title: Mirror-Symmetric Integer
statement:
Given an integer x, return true if its decimal digits read the same from left to right and from right to left, and false otherwise.

A negative number is never symmetric, because the minus sign only appears on the left. Try to solve it with arithmetic, without turning the number into a string.

examples.why: Written backwards it is "44-", which is not the same text.
Reversed it would be "03". A number cannot start with 0, so any number ending in 0 (other than 0 itself) fails.

hints: Negative numbers and numbers ending in 0 (except 0) can be rejected right away. Why?
x % 10 gives the last digit and Math.floor(x / 10) drops it. You can build the reverse of x digit by digit.
Reversing the whole number risks overflow in some languages. Reverse only the back half: stop when the reversed part is at least as large as what is left, then compare.

explain.intuition:
Peel digits off the end with % 10 and push them onto a new number with rev * 10 + digit. That builds the number backwards. If you reverse only until the reversed part catches up with the remaining part, you have split the number into a front half and a reversed back half, and the two must be equal.

With an odd number of digits the middle digit ends up in the reversed half. It does not matter what it is, so drop it with Math.floor(rev / 10) before comparing. Stopping at the halfway point also means the reversed value never grows past the original, which avoids overflow in fixed-width languages.
steps: If x < 0, or x ends in 0 and is not 0, return false.
Set rev = 0. While x > rev: rev = rev * 10 + x % 10, x = floor(x / 10).
Return x === rev (even length) or x === floor(rev / 10) (odd length).
pitfalls: Forgetting the trailing-zero check. For 10, the half-reverse loop ends with x = 0, rev = 1, and floor(rev / 10) = 0 wrongly matches.
Treating -121 as symmetric by taking the absolute value.
Using x / 10 in JavaScript without flooring, which gives fractions.

solutions.title: Compare the string with its reverse
solutions.idea: Write the number as text and check that it equals its reverse. Simple, but uses extra memory and skips the arithmetic the interviewer usually asks for.

solutions.title: Reverse half of the digits
solutions.idea: Move digits from the end of x onto a reversed number until the reversed part is at least as big, then compare the two halves.

followups: Check whether the number is symmetric in binary instead of decimal.
Find the smallest symmetric number that is greater than x.
